title: A branching growth beside the great toenail
task_type: A branching growth beside the great toenail
summary: A 23-year-old male marathon runner has a slowly enlarging, painless growth beside his left great toenail. It first appeared after a marathon approximately one year earlier. Examination describes a single firm, flesh-coloured nodule, about 0.8 × 0.5 × 0.3 cm, beneath the proximal/lateral nail fold. It has five finger-like keratotic projections, a collarette at the base and an associated longitudinal nail split; the rest of the nail plate appears preserved. There is no notable medical history, reported family history of a neurocutaneous disorder or other reported features of tuberous sclerosis. Histology and subsequent treatment results are not available at this decision point.
purpose: Write 160–220 words for a clinician. Summarise the lesion, compare up to three useful explanations and state what further assessment would distinguish them. Explain how much weight to give the solitary lesion, local mechanical exposure and absence of other reported syndromic features. Separate a plausible explanation from a confirmed diagnosis. Do not invent dermoscopic or histological findings, claim a syndrome has been definitively excluded or specify a surgical procedure. Give brief clinical justifications rather than a private reasoning trace.

- **Discussion, final paragraph:** two-month healing and a later, unconfirmed report of focal tissue change. This qualifies the shorter initial description of no recurrence.

case.hidden:
Adaptation and hidden information

The written description is paraphrased from the clinical text and published caption, rather than a new interpretation of the photograph. The task stops before excision; the source's multiple-choice options are removed. The source title, diagnosis, histology, immunostaining, procedure and follow-up are hidden during generation.

The article identifies a multibranched acquired periungual fibrokeratoma. Histology describes hyperkeratosis/acanthosis and longitudinal collagen, while CD34 staining is focal in vessels rather than diffusely positive in spindle cells. The discussion includes Koenen tumours, cellular digital fibroma and periungual warts as alternatives. The short case paragraph reports healing without recurrence; the final discussion also records suspected focal change at six months requiring confirmation. These follow-up statements should not be flattened into proven long-term cure.

### Reference and review — awaiting confirmation

Candidate review points are an accurate description of the solitary nail-unit lesion, a proportionate differential and a justified route to clarification. Temporal association with running does not independently establish causation. Absence of reported syndromic features supports an interpretation but is not a substitute for the relevant assessment. The hidden pathology must not be demanded as if the model had already seen it.

**Candidate rubric items:** D1 (factual accuracy), D3a (problem representation), D3b (hypotheses), D5u (uncertainty). D5c is not selected: this is a written task without executed information requests.

**Confirmation needed:** Which alternatives and further observations are essential at this decision point? How specific can the diagnosis reasonably be without histology? Is this textual morphology sufficient, or should a later image-enabled evaluation provide the original photograph?
